html:
The great mosque of Timbuktu, built of mud brick and timber in 1327. Mansa Musa of the Mali Empire ordered it on his way home from the pilgrimage to Mecca. Tradition names its designer as Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, a poet and architect from Andalusia who came back with the king.

The mosque made Timbuktu a place of learning as well as trade. With the Sankore and Sidi Yahia mosques it formed the core of the city's scholarly life, the world that produced the Timbuktu manuscripts. It was rebuilt and enlarged in the 1570s under the Songhai Empire.

Mud walls wash away in the rains, so the building lives by regular replastering, as at the Great Mosque of Djenné. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1988.
